We compute the Laurent expansion of $f(z) = \dfrac{1}{z^2 \sin z}$ about $z=0$.

Recall the Taylor series
$$\sin z = z - \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^5}{120} - \cdots = z\left(1 - \frac{z^2}{6} + \frac{z^4}{120} - \cdots\right).$$

Therefore
$$z^2 \sin z = z^2 \cdot z\left(1 - \frac{z^2}{6} + \cdots\right) = z^3\left(1 - \frac{z^2}{6} + \cdots\right).$$

Hence
$$f(z) = \frac{1}{z^3\left(1 - \frac{z^2}{6} + \cdots\right)} = \frac{1}{z^3}\cdot\frac{1}{1 - \frac{z^2}{6} + \cdots}.$$

Using $\frac{1}{1-u} = 1 + u + u^2 + \cdots$ with $u = \frac{z^2}{6} - \cdots$,
$$\frac{1}{1 - \frac{z^2}{6} + \cdots} = 1 + \frac{z^2}{6} + \cdots,$$

so
$$f(z) = \frac{1}{z^3}\left(1 + \frac{z^2}{6} + \cdots\right) = \frac{1}{z^3} + \frac{1}{6z} + \cdots.$$

The residue at $z=0$ is the coefficient of $\dfrac{1}{z}$ in the Laurent expansion, which is

$$\boxed{\dfrac{1}{6}}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
